title: State of the tech job market: late 2026
text: State of the tech job market: late 2026 Subscribe Sign in State of the tech job market: late 2026 PMs are winning, engineers are plateauing, designers are hurting, and the biggest AI hiring boom isn’t in software Lenny Rachitsky Nov 10, 2026 ∙ Paid 227 19 21 Share 👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Jobs | Lenny’s Podcast | Lennybot | How I AI | Become an AI-Native Builder and my other favorite AI/PM courses . Subscribe P.S. Get a full free year of Cursor, Notion, Replit, Lovable, Wispr Flow, Linear, ElevenLabs, PostHog, Granola, Brain.fm, Waking Up, and more, by becoming an Insider subscriber (while supplies last). Learn more . Welcome to my latest job market report, my second of 2026. Of the five reports I’ve done over the past few years, this one is the most surprising and interesting. Here’s what we’re seeing right now: PMs seem to be winning in the AI era Engineering demand has stalled Design is at a record low Everybody now needs to AI Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area Remote is at a record low The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!) This analysis is based on two proprietary datasets that I love working with: TrueUp , which powers Lenny’s Jobs and tracks global job openings at tech companies (over 9,000 companies). The second dataset comes from Live Data Technologies , which tracks job changes (hires, departures, and promotions) for 124 million professionals, and their hiring numbers below are specifically for the U.S. Looking at these together, we can triangulate common trends, and the differences between the datasets are themselves revealing. Thank you, Amit Taylor and Alex Hamilton , for sharing this amazing data with us. 🙏 Let’s get into it. P.S. If you’re looking for a job, check out Lenny’s Jobs ! Takeaway 1: Product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era There’s been a lot of talk about AI replacing product managers (“who needs ’em!”). But so far, the data is showing the exact opposite. There are more open PM roles than at any point in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings have grown faster than any other core tech role since the start of 2023 (+56%, compared with +43% for engineering). When we look at hiring numbers vs. just job openings, the story gets more interesting. Even though open roles are growing, actual hiring for every core product role has been flat or in decline over the past few years (see takeaway 7 for which roles are now growing fastest). But PM hiring has held up the best (by far). And PM is the only one of the five core roles whose share of hiring grew (from 16% in 2021 to 21% today). The fact that we’re seeing growth in PM openings (first set of charts) but a flat line and even a decline in hiring (second set of charts) tells me that there’s growing demand for PMs, but that landing great PMs is getting harder. Takeaway 2: Demand for engineers is plateauing For the first time in the history of this report, engineering job openings have stalled. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% this past year . There are fewer open eng roles at tech companies today than there were even this past March. The hiring data shows the same slowdown. Companies in the U.S. hired about 113,000 software engineers over the past 12 months (May 2025 to April 2026)—less than half the 2022 peak (239,000). And the number has dropped every year since 2022. Just like with PMs, engineering job openings are up while actual hiring is down (+44% vs. −17% since January 2024), so even as demand slows, landing great engineers is getting harder too. Two bright spots for engineers: One, demand for tech recruiters is on an absolute tear. We’re hitting record highs: open recruiter roles are up nearly 300% since mid-2023. This may be a leading indicator of a reacceleration of eng hiring, which we’ll be watching closely. Another bright spot is that in terms of absolute numbers, engineering is still the largest category of tech hiring, by far. Over 120,000 engineers were hired just in the U.S. in 2025. And there are still plenty of great engineering jobs out there. Over 65,000 to be exact . One additional new trend to watch within the engineering function is the rise of the forward deployed engineer (FDE) . FDE openings are exploding. Historically, there have been only a few dozen open FDE roles globally (mostly at Palantir), but openings started climbing in 2025 and are up 4.6x in the past year alone! There are currently around 1,500 open FDE roles . Note that this growth is likely a combination of increased demand for this job along with other job categories, like “sales engineer,” being rebranded as “FDE.” Either way, FDE is so hot right now. Also, a telling trend: security engineering is one of the fastest-growing specialties, right behind FDEs. On the flip side, demand for mobile and front-end engineers has been nearly halved in the past year. That’s wild. I think the story here is the collapse of specialized/siloed engineering disciplines, with smaller eng teams having broader ownership (thanks to AI). Takeaway 3: Demand for designers continues to hit record lows Unfortunately for my designer friends, design roles continue to decline. There are only about 1,900 open product design roles 1 at tech companies globally right now. Not that much higher than just open FDE roles. It’s the lowest we’ve seen since we started tracking, and down 28% from a year ago. 😥 Actual hiring data from Live Data Technologies tells the same story. U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers over the past 12 months, less than half as many as in 2022 (27,600), and the number has fallen every year since. Even more telling, the ratio of open PM roles to open design roles is trending further and further toward PM. There are now 3.8 open PM roles for every open design role.
